title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension
claim: A one-dimensional convex function's geometry near its minimizer defines an instance-dependent gap that sets the difficulty of localizing the minimizer.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right plot, shaded interval with brace and gap arrows
description: A single hand-drawn plot of a piecewise-linear convex function f on [0,1]. The curve falls with a gentle slope to its minimizer x_star, then rises steeply to the right. Black dots mark the minimizer and two points at equal height on either side of it. An orange dot labeled z_epsilon sits on the descending branch between them. A light-blue shaded band with dashed navy borders and a brace on top, labeled with a set symbol, marks the interval around the minimizer. Gray dashed horizontal lines mark the minimum value f_star and the higher level of the two outer points. A vertical double arrow between them is labeled Delta_epsilon(f). Horizontal double arrows at the bottom mark two epsilon-length distances. The eye goes first to the black V-shaped curve, then to the shaded band and the orange point.
caption: Example of a convex function f ∈Funq and of the geometry around its minimizer x⋆. The point zε maximizes min( ¯f(z −ε), ¯f(z + ε)) over z ∈X d
abstract: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $Î_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $Î_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.
